metadata.title: On the Behavior of Tile Assembly System at High Temperatures

nodes.name: $\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms
nodes.statement: This motivates us to study a system of inequalities whose left-hand side consists of at most 4 terms (non-negative integers or constants) and whose right-hand side is $\tau$. We call such an inequality a {\it $\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms}; we use this term often with the replacement of $\tau$ by either $\ge_\tau$ (at least $\tau$) or $<_\tau$ (strictly less than $\tau$) to specify its sign.
nodes.statement_short: An inequality with at most 4 non-negative-integer terms on the left and the temperature $\tau$ on the right, signed $\ge_\tau$ or $<_\tau$.
nodes.genus: a system of inequalities whose left-hand side consists of at most 4 terms
differentia: at most 4 terms (non-negative integers or constants)
whose right-hand side is $\tau$

nodes.name: tile complexity
nodes.statement: There and also in this paper, the optimality of TASs is measured by the number of distinct tile types they contain, and this criterion is called the {\it tile complexity}.
nodes.genus: the number of distinct tile types they contain

nodes.name: full grid graph
nodes.statement: Given a set of points $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ on the integer lattice, the {\it full grid graph} of $A$ is the undirected graph $G^{\rm f}_A = (V, E)$, where $V = A$ and for all $u, v \in V$, there is an edge between $u$ and $v$ if and only if $||u-v||_2 = 1$, where $|| \cdot ||_2$ is the Manhattan distance, that is, $u$ and $v$ are adjacent points.
nodes.statement_short: The graph on a point set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ joining points at Manhattan distance 1.
differentia: $V = A$
for all $u, v \in V$, there is an edge between $u$ and $v$ if and only if $||u-v||_2 = 1$

nodes.name: shape
nodes.statement: A {\it shape} is a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ such that $G^{\rm f}_S$ is connected, and we denote the set of all {\it finite} shapes by $\mathcal{FS} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{Z}^2)$.
differentia: $G^{\rm f}_S$ is connected

nodes.name: tile type
nodes.statement: A {\it tile type} $t$ is a quadruple $t \in \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^* \times \Sigma^*$, and is regarded as a unit square with four sides listed in the counter-clockwise order starting at the north (\north), each having a {\it glue label} (a.k.a., {\it glue}) taken from $\Sigma^*$.
nodes.statement_short: A unit square whose four sides, listed counter-clockwise from the north, each carry a glue label from $\Sigma^*$.
differentia: is regarded as a unit square with four sides listed in the counter-clockwise order starting at the north (\north), each having a {\it glue label} (a.k.a., {\it glue}) taken from $\Sigma^*$

nodes.name: assembly (supertile)
nodes.statement: An {\it assembly} (a.k.a., {\it supertile}) is a positioning of tiles of types in $T$ on (part of) the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. It does not have to be a tessellation. Hence, we can say that an assembly is a partial function $\mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$.
nodes.genus: a positioning of tiles of types in $T$ on (part of) the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$
differentia: It does not have to be a tessellation

nodes.name: sub-assembly
nodes.statement: Given two assemblies $\alpha, \beta: \mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$, $\alpha$ is a {\it sub-assembly} of $\beta$, written as $\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta$, if $\dom(\alpha) \subseteq \dom(\beta)$ and for every point $p \in \dom(\alpha)$, $\alpha(p) = \beta(p)$, where $\dom$ denotes the domain of the function.
differentia: $\dom(\alpha) \subseteq \dom(\beta)$
for every point $p \in \dom(\alpha)$, $\alpha(p) = \beta(p)$

nodes.name: strength function
nodes.statement: A {\it strength function $g: \Lambda(T) \to \mathbb{N}_0$} endows tiles with an ability to interact with its neighboring tiles by assigning the strength $g(\ell)$ to the {\it matching} label $\ell$ of their abutting edges. If the labels do not match or $g(\ell) = 0$, these tiles do not interact; otherwise, they do.
nodes.statement_short: A map from glue labels to non-negative integers giving the binding strength of matching abutting edges.
differentia: assigning the strength $g(\ell)$ to the {\it matching} label $\ell$ of their abutting edges
If the labels do not match or $g(\ell) = 0$, these tiles do not interact

nodes.name: binding graph
nodes.statement: An assembly $\alpha$ and a strength function $g$ induce a {\it binding graph}, which is a grid graph whose vertices are $\dom(\alpha)$ and for two neighboring positions $p_1, p_2 \in \dom(\alpha)$, there is an edge between $p_1$ and $p_2$ on this graph if and only if the tiles $\alpha(p_1)$ and $\alpha(p_2)$ interact. On this graph, an edge between vertices means that the corresponding tiles interact, and hence, their abutting edges share the same label $\ell$. Thus, we can consider that the edge is labeled with $\ell$ and $g$ gives it the weight $g(\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: The weighted grid graph on $\dom(\alpha)$ whose edges join interacting neighbours, weighted by glue strength.
nodes.genus: a grid graph whose vertices are $\dom(\alpha)$
differentia: for two neighboring positions $p_1, p_2 \in \dom(\alpha)$, there is an edge between $p_1$ and $p_2$ on this graph if and only if the tiles $\alpha(p_1)$ and $\alpha(p_2)$ interact

nodes.name: $\tau$-stable assembly
nodes.statement: The assembly is {\it $\tau$-stable (with respect to $g$)} if every cut of its binding graph has strength at least $\tau$. That is, the assembly is $\tau$-stable if at least energy $\tau$ is required to separate it into two parts.
differentia: every cut of its binding graph has strength at least $\tau$

nodes.name: (seeded) tile assembly system (TAS)
nodes.statement: A {\it (seeded) tile assembly system} (TAS) is a quadruple $\tas = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$, where $T$ and $g$ are as stated above, $\sigma: \mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$ is a finite $\tau$-stable {\it seed assembly}, and $\tau \ge 1$ is an integer parameter called {\it temperature}. TASs are provided with inexhaustible supply of copies of each tile type, each copy being referred to as a {\it tile}.
nodes.statement_short: A quadruple $\tas = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ of tile types, a $\tau$-stable seed assembly, a strength function, and an integer temperature.
differentia: $\sigma: \mathbb{Z}^2 \dashrightarrow T$ is a finite $\tau$-stable {\it seed assembly}
$\tau \ge 1$ is an integer parameter called {\it temperature}

nodes.name: singly-seeded TAS
nodes.statement: If the seed assembly $\sigma$ consists of a single tile, then $\tas$ is said to be {\it singly-seeded}.
differentia: the seed assembly $\sigma$ consists of a single tile

nodes.name: $\tas$-produces in one step
nodes.statement: Given two $\tau$-stable assemblies $\alpha, \beta$, we write $\alpha \to_1^{\tas} \beta$ if $\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta$ and $\dom(\beta) \setminus \dom(\alpha) = \{p\}$ for some position $p \in \mathbb{Z}^2$. Intuitively, this means that $\alpha$ can grow into $\beta$ by the addition of a single tile at the position $p$. Since $\beta$ is required to be $\tau$-stable, the new tile is able to bind to $\alpha$ with strength at least $\tau$. In this case, we say that {\it $\alpha$ $\tas$-produces $\beta$ in one step}.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha \to_1^{\tas} \beta$ when $\beta$ extends $\alpha$ by a single $\tau$-stably attached tile.
differentia: $\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta$ and $\dom(\beta) \setminus \dom(\alpha) = \{p\}$ for some position $p \in \mathbb{Z}^2$
the new tile is able to bind to $\alpha$ with strength at least $\tau$

nodes.name: $\tas$-assembly sequence and $\tas$-produces
nodes.statement: A sequence of $\tau$-stable assemblies $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k$ is a {\it $\tas$-assembly sequence} if for all $1 \le i \le k$, $\alpha_{i-1} \to_1^{\tas} \alpha_i$ holds. We write $\alpha \to^\tas \beta$ and say {\it $\alpha$ $\tas$-produces $\beta$} (in 0 or more steps) if there is a $\tas$-assembly sequence $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k$ of length $k = |\dom(\beta) \setminus \dom(\alpha)|$ with $\alpha_0 = \alpha$ and $\alpha_k = \beta$.
nodes.statement_short: A chain of single-tile additions; $\alpha \to^\tas \beta$ means such a chain of the right length joins $\alpha$ to $\beta$.
differentia: for all $1 \le i \le k$, $\alpha_{i-1} \to_1^{\tas} \alpha_i$ holds

nodes.name: $\tas$-producible and terminal assemblies
nodes.statement: An assembly $\alpha$ is {\it $\tas$-producible} or {\it producible by $\tas$} if $\sigma \to^\tas \alpha$. A $\tau$-stable assembly $\alpha$ is {\it ($\tas$-)terminal} if for any $\tau$-stable assembly $\beta$, $\alpha \to^\tas \beta$ implies $\alpha = \beta$. Let $\mathcal{A}[\tas]$ be the set of assemblies producible by $\tas$, and let $\mathcal{A}_\Box[\tas] \subseteq \mathcal{A}[\tas]$ be the set of terminal assemblies that are producible by $\tas$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha$ is producible if $\sigma \to^\tas \alpha$, and terminal if it produces only itself; $\mathcal{A}[\tas]$ and $\mathcal{A}_\Box[\tas]$ collect them.
differentia: $\sigma \to^\tas \alpha$
for any $\tau$-stable assembly $\beta$, $\alpha \to^\tas \beta$ implies $\alpha = \beta$

nodes.name: directed TAS
nodes.statement: A TAS $\tas$ is {\it directed} if the poset $(\mathcal{A}[\tas], \to^\tas)$ is directed, i.e., for each $\alpha, \beta \in \mathcal{A}[\tas]$, there exists $\gamma \in \mathcal{A}[\tas]$ such that $\alpha \to^\tas \gamma$ and $\beta \to^\tas \gamma$.
differentia: the poset $(\mathcal{A}[\tas], \to^\tas)$ is directed, i.e., for each $\alpha, \beta \in \mathcal{A}[\tas]$, there exists $\gamma \in \mathcal{A}[\tas]$ such that $\alpha \to^\tas \gamma$ and $\beta \to^\tas \gamma$

nodes.name: strictly (uniquely) self-assembles
nodes.statement: Given a shape $S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$, a TAS $\tas$ {\it strictly (a.k.a.,~uniquely) (self-)assembles} $S$ if the shape of every terminal assembly produced by $\tas$ is $S$.
differentia: the shape of every terminal assembly produced by $\tas$ is $S$

nodes.name: temperature-2 directed tile complexity
nodes.statement: The {\it temperature-2 directed tile complexity} of $S$ is formally defined as follows: \[ \dtilec{2}(S) = \min \biggl\{|T| \left| \begin{array}{r} \mbox{$\tas = (T, \sigma, g, 2)$ is a directed TAS} \\ \mbox{that strictly self-assembles $S$} \end{array} \right\}. \] This is the minimum number of tile types required for a directed TAS at the temperature 2 to strictly self-assemble $S$.
nodes.statement_short: $\dtilec{2}(S)$ is the least number of tile types of a directed temperature-2 TAS that strictly self-assembles $S$.
nodes.genus: the minimum number of tile types required for a directed TAS at the temperature 2 to strictly self-assemble $S$

nodes.name: directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperature $\tau$
nodes.statement: We parameterize this complexity measure by a temperature $\tau$ as: \[ \dtilec{\tau}(S) = \min \biggl\{|T| \left| \begin{array}{r} \mbox{$\tas = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ is a directed TAS} \\ \mbox{that strictly self-assembles $S$} \end{array} \right\}, \] and introduce it as {\it directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperature $\tau$}.
nodes.statement_short: $\dtilec{\tau}(S)$ is $\dtilec{2}$ generalized to an arbitrary temperature parameter $\tau$.
nodes.definiendum: directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperature $\tau$
differentia: $\tas = (T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ is a directed TAS

nodes.name: directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperatures at most $\tau$
nodes.statement: This non-monotonicity motivates us to introduce the notion of {\it directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperatures at most $\tau$}. This measure is to be defined as \[ \dtilec{\le \tau}(S) = \min\{\dtilec{i}(S) \mid 1 \le i \le \tau\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\dtilec{\le \tau}(S)$ is the minimum of $\dtilec{i}(S)$ over all temperatures $1 \le i \le \tau$.
nodes.definiendum: directed tile complexity of $S$ at the temperatures at most $\tau$

nodes.name: cooperation set of $t$ with respect to $g$ and $\tau$
nodes.statement: More precisely, $g$ and $\tau$ do so by specifying the local behavior of each tile type $t \in T$ in the form of {\it cooperation set of $t$ with respect to $g$ and $\tau$} \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}, which is defined as: \[ \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t) = \Bigl\{ D \subseteq \{\north, \west, \south, \east\} \Bigm| \mbox{$\sum_{d \in D} g(t(d)) \ge \tau$} \Bigr\}. \] This is the collection of sets of four sides of $t$ whose glues have sufficient strengths to bind $t$ cooperatively.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{D}_{g,\tau}(t)$ collects the side-subsets of a tile type whose glue strengths sum to at least $\tau$.
nodes.definiendum: cooperation set of $t$ with respect to $g$ and $\tau$
nodes.genus: the collection of sets of four sides of $t$
differentia: \mbox{$\sum_{d \in D} g(t(d)) \ge \tau$}

nodes.name: locally equivalent TASs
nodes.statement: Given $\tas_1 = (T, \sigma, g_1, \tau_1)$ and $\tas_2 = (T, \sigma, g_2, \tau_2)$ that share the tile set $T$ and seed $\sigma$, if $\mathcal{D}_{g_1, \tau_1}(t) = \mathcal{D}_{g_2, \tau_2}(t)$ for each tile type $t \in T$, then these TASs are said to be {\it locally equivalent} (written as $\tas_1 \sim \tas_2$) \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}.
nodes.statement_short: Two TASs sharing tile set and seed are locally equivalent when all their cooperation sets agree.
differentia: share the tile set $T$ and seed $\sigma$
$\mathcal{D}_{g_1, \tau_1}(t) = \mathcal{D}_{g_2, \tau_2}(t)$ for each tile type $t \in T$

nodes.name: strength-free TAS
nodes.statement: Chen, Doty, and Seki introduced this variant called {\it strength-free TAS} \cite{ChenDotySeki2011} as it is free from strength function or temperature. Formally, a {\it strength-free TAS} is a triple $(T, \sigma, \mathcal{D})$, where $T$ and $\sigma$ are the same as those for TAS, while $\mathcal{D}: T \to \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\{\north, \west, \south, \east\}))$ is a function from a tile type $t \in T$ to a set of subsets of $\{\north, \west, \south, \east\}$ that is closed under superset operation, where $\mathcal{P}$ means the power set.
nodes.statement_short: A triple $(T, \sigma, \mathcal{D})$ replacing strength function and temperature by superset-closed cooperation sets.
differentia: $\mathcal{D}: T \to \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(\{\north, \west, \south, \east\}))$ is a function from a tile type $t \in T$ to a set of subsets of $\{\north, \west, \south, \east\}$ that is closed under superset operation

nodes.name: local equivalence between a TAS and a strength-free TAS
nodes.statement: As done between TASs, we can define the local equivalence between a TAS $(T, \sigma, g, \tau)$ and a strength-free TAS $\tas_{\rm sf} = (T, \sigma, \mathcal{D})$ as: they are {\it locally-equivalent} if $\mathcal{D}(t) = \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$ for each $t \in T$.
differentia: $\mathcal{D}(t) = \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$ for each $t \in T$

nodes.name: $2^{i+1}$-adder (to the lower bound of a variable)
nodes.statement: Let us build a sub-system called {\it $2^{i+1}$-adder (to the lower bound of a variable)}. Based on a variable $x$ with a lower bound $n$, i.e., $x \ge n$, it aims at creating another variable with a lower bound $n+2^{i+1}$. Using $5i{+}5$ positive integer variables $z_1, z_2, x_0, x_b, x_c, A_k, A_k', A_k'', B_k', B_k'' (1 \le k \le i)$, we design the $2^{i+1}$-adder as follows: for $2 \le j \le i$, \begin{equation} \begin{array}{llll} A_1' + B_1' + x_0, & A_1'' + B_1'' + x_0 &\ge& \tau, \\ A_1 + B_1' + x_0, & A_1' + B_1'' + x_0 &<& \tau, \\ A_{j-1} + B_j' + A_j', & A_{j-1} + B_j'' + A_j'' &\ge& \tau, \\ A_{j-1}'' + B_j' + A_j, & A_j' + B_j'' + A_{j-1}'' &<& \tau, \\ A_i'' + x_b, & z_1 + x_c &<& \tau, \\ z_1 + x_b, & z_2 + x_c &\ge& \tau. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A sub-system of three-term $\tau$-inequalities on $5i{+}5$ positive variables that turns a lower bound $n$ into a lower bound $n+2^{i+1}$.
nodes.definiendum: $2^{i+1}$-adder (to the lower bound of a variable)
differentia: Based on a variable $x$ with a lower bound $n$, i.e., $x \ge n$, it aims at creating another variable with a lower bound $n+2^{i+1}$
Using $5i{+}5$ positive integer variables $z_1, z_2, x_0, x_b, x_c, A_k, A_k', A_k'', B_k', B_k'' (1 \le k \le i)$

nodes.name: quadripartite system of $\tau$-inequalities
nodes.statement: We say that a system of $\tau$-inequalities is {\it quadripartite} if \begin{enumerate} \item every inequality in it consists of at most {\it four} terms; \item its variable set can be partitioned into four disjoint subsets so that distinct terms of each inequality belong to distinct subsets. \end{enumerate} (The first condition follows from the second and hence not necessary.)
nodes.statement_short: A $\tau$-inequality system whose variables split into four classes with each inequality using at most one variable per class.
differentia: every inequality in it consists of at most {\it four} terms
its variable set can be partitioned into four disjoint subsets so that distinct terms of each inequality belong to distinct subsets

nodes.name: variable trees (north, west, south, east type)
nodes.statement:
In this step, we convert each variable in $V$ into one of the four tree shapes illustrated in Figure~ef{fig:4vars_atleast_tau} depending on which of $V_
orth, V_\west, V_\south, V_\east$ it belongs to. For instance, each variable in $V_
orth$ is converted into the shape whose tip is numbered 1 (and colored red). This shape is a tree of height $h$ plus some constant, not depending on $h$, with only one crotch for two branches; one consists of a bit pattern and the other is of size 1 for cooperation called {\it cooperation tip}, which is numbered 1 in Figure~ef{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}. We say that this shape is of {\it north type} after the subscript of $V_
orth$. Shapes of north type that are thus converted from distinct variables (in $V_
orth$) are identical mod their bit patterns of length $\lceil \log n ceil$. In this way, each variable in the other three variable subsets $V_\west, V_\south, V_\east$ is also converted into the shapes that are numbered 2, 3, 4 (and colored yellow, green, blue) in Figure~ef{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}, respectively, and we say that these shapes are respectively of {\it west, south, and east type}. All the $n$ variables of $V$ have been now associated with $n$ different tree shapes of proper type. We collectively refer to them as {\it variable trees}.
nodes.statement_short: Each variable becomes a height-$h$ tree shape whose type encodes its quadripartite class and whose bit pattern encodes its identity, with a single cooperation tip.
nodes.genus: a tree of height $h$ plus some constant, not depending on $h$
differentia: with only one crotch for two branches; one consists of a bit pattern and the other is of size 1 for cooperation called {\it cooperation tip}
Shapes of north type that are thus converted from distinct variables (in $V_\north$) are identical mod their bit patterns of length $\lceil \log n \rceil$

nodes.name: auxiliary tree
nodes.statement: Every conversion of $<_\tau$-inequalities in $\mathcal{S}$ into logical components at Step~3 needs to introduce an auxiliary tree of the north, west, south, or east type and recall that $\mathcal{S}$ was assumed to contain $c'$ of them (the conversion of $\ge_\tau$-inequalities does not). These trees are distinguished from each other and from the variable trees by their bit patterns. Two copies of each auxiliary tree are mounted next to each other on the scaffold of $S$. We will call variable trees and auxiliary trees simply trees unless confusion arises.
nodes.statement_short: One extra tree per $<_\tau$-inequality, of a type distinct from the inequality's variable trees and distinguished by its bit pattern.
nodes.genus: an auxiliary tree of the north, west, south, or east type
differentia: These trees are distinguished from each other and from the variable trees by their bit patterns

nodes.name: logical component
nodes.statement: In this step, we convert $\ge_\tau$-inequalities and $<_\tau$-inequalities of the given system $\mathcal{S}$ into shapes which we call {\it logical components}. Two of their copies will be mounted in Step 4 onto the scaffold, which will complete the design of the shape $S$.
nodes.statement_short: The shape into which one $\tau$-inequality is converted, built by bundling the trees of its variables (its pillars).

nodes.name: the label $\ell_i$ at the cooperation tip of $t_i$
nodes.statement: Now, for $1 \le i \le n$, we can denote {\it the} tile type that $\tas$ puts at the both cooperation tips of the copies of the variable tree for $v_i$ by $t_i$. The label $\ell_i$ mentioned in Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver} is found at the side of $t_i$ opposite to the crotch. That is, \[ \ell_i = \begin{cases} t_i(\south) & \text{if $v_i \in V_\north$} \\ t_i(\east) & \text{if $v_i \in V_\west$} \\ t_i(\north) & \text{if $v_i \in V_\south$} \\ t_i(\west) & \text{if $v_i \in V_\east$}. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: $\ell_i$ is the glue of $t_i$ on the side opposite the crotch, chosen per the quadripartite class of $v_i$.
differentia: The label $\ell_i$ mentioned in Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver} is found at the side of $t_i$ opposite to the crotch

nodes.name: integrality of glue strengths and temperature
nodes.statement: Conventionally, the glue strengths (and hence, temperature) of TASs are assumed to be integers, without loss of generality. Indeed, this is a way of ``quantizing'' the minimum distinction we are willing to make between energies and then re-scalling so that this quantity is normalized to 1.
nodes.statement_short: Glue strengths and $\tau$ are taken to be integers, a quantization of the smallest distinguishable energy gap.

nodes.name: only singly-seeded TASs are considered
nodes.statement: In this paper, we consider only singly-seeded TASs.

nodes.name: full side set lies in every cooperation set
nodes.statement: Combining these together, we assume that for any $t \in T$, $\{\north, \west, \south, \east\} \in \mathcal{D}_{g, \tau}(t)$.

nodes.name: positive variables are made positive via \eqref{eq:positive}
nodes.statement: In the rest, when we say that a system has a positive variable $x$, we assume that its positiveness is guaranteed in this way.

nodes.name: every variable is strictly less than $\tau$
nodes.statement: As mentioned in Remark~\ref{rmk:strictly_lessthan_tau}, we can assume that every variable in $V$ is {\it strictly} less than $\tau$; this assumption simplifies the design of $S$ and our explanation below.

nodes.name: 0-1 integer programming
nodes.statement: 0-1 integer programming, one of the Karp's 21 \NP-complete problems \cite{Karp1972}, is a decision variant of integer programming in which all the variables are restricted to be binary. In order to prove the completeness, Karp employed a polynomial-time reduction from the Boolean satisfiability problem ($\SAT$) to this problem.

nodes.name: \findstrength
nodes.statement: This implementability check was formalized as $\findstrength$ in \cite{ChenDotySeki2011}, which is defined as follows: \[ \begin{array}{l} \findstrength \\ \begin{array}{ll} {\tt INPUT:} & \mbox{a strength-free TAS $\tas_{\rm sf}$} \\ {\tt OUTPUT:} & \mbox{a TAS that is locally equivalent to $\tas_{\rm sf}$, if any,}\\ & \mbox{or reports that none of such TAS exists otherwise}. \end{array} \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Given a strength-free TAS, output a locally equivalent TAS or report that none exists.
output: a TAS that is locally equivalent to $\tas_{\rm sf}$, if any,

nodes.name: \findoptstrength
nodes.statement: This motivates us to study the following optimization: \[ \begin{array}{l} \findoptstrength \\ \begin{array}{ll} {\tt INPUT:} & \mbox{a strength-free TAS $\tas_{\rm sf}$} \\ {\tt OUTPUT:} & \mbox{a TAS of minimal temperature that is locally equivalent to $\tas_{\rm sf}$} \\ & \mbox{if any, or reports that none of such TAS exists otherwise}. \end{array} \end{array} \]
nodes.statement_short: Given a strength-free TAS, output a locally equivalent TAS of minimal temperature, or report that none exists.
output: a TAS of minimal temperature that is locally equivalent to $\tas_{\rm sf}$

nodes.name: threshold programming (TP)
nodes.statement: In order to prove the \NP-hardness of $\findoptstrength$, let us introduce a subclass of integer programming (IP) that aims at optimizing $\tau$ subject to only $\ge_\tau$-inequalities and $<_\tau$-inequalities. We call such an IP a {\it threshold programming} (TP). This is formalized as: for given integer matrices $C_1, C_2$, minimize $\tau$ on condition that there exists a nonnegative integer vector $\Vec{x}$ satisfying \[ \mbox{$C_1 \vec{x} \ge \tau \Vec{1}$ ($\ge_\tau$-inequalities) and $C_2 \vec{x} < \tau \Vec{1}$ ($<_\tau$-inequalities)}, \] where $\Vec{1}$ is the vector all of whose components are 1.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize $\tau$ subject to $C_1\vec{x} \ge \tau\Vec{1}$ and $C_2\vec{x} < \tau\Vec{1}$ over non-negative integer $\vec{x}$.
output: minimize $\tau$ on condition that there exists a nonnegative integer vector $\Vec{x}$ satisfying

nodes.name: TP(4,~3) and its decision variant $\tau$-TP(4,~3)
nodes.statement: We denote the class of TPs any of whose constraints contains at most the number of terms as specified above by TP(4,~3). Its decision variant, denoted by $\tau$-$\TP(4, 3)$ or simply $\tau$-TP(4,~3), is of interest in which $\tau$ is not a variable but a given constant, and one is asked to decide whether $\Vec{x}$ exists.
nodes.statement_short: TP restricted to $\ge_\tau$-inequalities of $\le 4$ terms and $<_\tau$-inequalities of $\le 3$ terms, plus its fixed-$\tau$ decision variant.

nodes.name: monotone \oneinthree
nodes.statement: For the reduction, we employ a variant of 3-$\SAT$ called monotone $\oneinthree$ introduced by Schaefer \cite{Schaefer1978}, in which no literal is negated (monotonicity) and one is required to find a truth assignment such that each clause has {\it exactly one} true literal.

nodes.name: quadripartite \oneinthree
nodes.statement: We propose its restricted variant called {\it quadripartite $\oneinthree$}, whose instance consists of a variable set that is a union of four pairwise disjoint sets $U_1, U_2, U_3, U_4$ and clauses that contain at most one variable from each of these four subsets.
nodes.statement_short: Monotone 1-in-3-SAT whose variables split into four disjoint classes, each clause using at most one variable per class.

nodes.name: removing the temperature upper bound
nodes.statement: The open problem was whether the temperature upper-bound could be removed.

nodes.statement: We propose the following unified approach to various problems related to the behaviors and temperatures of directed TASs including the above two problems: \begin{enumerate}[Step 1.] \item choose a quadripartite system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities properly for the purpose among those built in Section~\ref{sec:behavior}; hence, all $\ge_\tau$-inequalities of $\mathcal{S}$ are of at most 4 terms and all of its $<_\tau$-inequalities are of at most 3 terms; \item convert its variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ into trees of height $h$ and distinct shape, which we call {\it variable trees}, where $h$ is a parameter adjustable for our convenience; \item for each $\tau$-inequality, bundle the (at most 4) trees thus converted from its variables into a shape called the {\it logical component}; \item (two copies of) the $n$ variable trees and logical components each are mounted next to each other onto a scaffold, and amounts to a shape, which we denote by $S$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem ($\tau$-$\TP(4, 3)$ is \NP-complete)
nodes.statement: A proof for $\tau=4$ comes first. An instance of quadripartite\footnote{The quadripartite property is not needed here, but will be so in Section~\ref{sec:complexity}.} $\oneinthree$, whose \NP-completeness was proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:quad_1in3SAT}, will be reduced into an instance of $\tau$-TP(4,~3). Let us represent this instance as a pair of a set of Boolean variables $U = \{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}$ and that of clauses $C = \{c_1, \ldots, c_m\}$. Let us convert this SAT instance into a system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities with positive integer variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ (needless to say, \eqref{eq:positive} is used here for their positiveness), which correspond to the SAT variables in $U$, such that the SAT instance is satisfiable if and only if the system is solvable. In $\mathcal{S}$, the $j$-th clause of $C$, $c_j = \{u_{j_1}, u_{j_2}, u_{j_3}\}$ with $1 \le j_1, j_2, j_3 \le n$, is represented as \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < 4, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < 4, \end{equation} which is equivalent to the equation $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$ due to the assumption that $v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3} \ge 1$. Its solution must be that exactly one of the three variables is 2 and the others are 1. Therefore, if $\mathcal{S}$ is solvable, then by interpreting those in $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ with value 2 be positive and the other (that is, with value 1) negative, we can retrieve a way to satisfy the $\oneinthree$ instance; and vice versa. Thus, 4-TP(4, 3) is \NP-complete (in fact, we proved that even 4-TP(3, 2) is so, see \eqref{eq:clause_4}). Now the result is generalized for an arbitrary $\tau \ge 4$. In $\mathcal{S}$, we first embed systems of $\tau$-inequalities of at most three terms, presented in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries}, that provide auxiliary variables $x_1, x_2, x_{\tau{-}4}$ with lower bounds 1, 2, and $\tau{-}4$, respectively. Combining them with an inequality \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 + x_{\tau{-}4} < \tau \end{equation} yields $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 2$, and $x_{\tau{-}4} = \tau{-}4$. This means that by \eqref{eq:tau-4} being embedded, in any solution of $\mathcal{S}$, these variables must admit these respective values. Especially, the ``constant'' $x_{\tau{-}4}$ is added to the inequalities in \eqref{eq:clause_4}, and we obtain \begin{eqnarray} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} + x_{\tau{-}4} &\ge& \tau, \\ v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + x_{\tau{-}4} &<& \tau, \end{eqnarray} and the analogs of \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} for $v_{j_1} + v_{j_3}$ and $v_{j_2} + v_{j_3}$. Since $x_{\tau-4} = \tau-4$, these four $\tau$-inequalities are equivalent to $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$. We conclude this proof by noting that any $\tau$-inequality used is either a $\ge_\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms or a $<_\tau$-inequality of at most 3 terms, and the resulting system of $\tau$-inequalities is quadripartite. This quadripartite property will become critical in proving Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}.
nodes.statement_short: Encode each 1-in-3 clause as $v_{j_1}+v_{j_2}+v_{j_3}=4$ via four $\tau$-inequalities, then lift to arbitrary $\tau \ge 4$ by adding an adder-forced constant $x_{\tau-4}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma ($\TP(4, 3)$ is \NP-hard)
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} leads us to the \NP-hardness of TP. Deleting the constant term $x_{\tau-4}$ from the inequalities \eqref{eq:tau-4}, \eqref{eq:clause_atleast_tau}, and \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} yields the following inequalities: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 < \tau, \end{equation} \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < \tau, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < \tau. \end{equation} Consider optimizing $\tau$ subject to these. Due to \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2}, the minimal possible value of $\tau$ is 4. Then its optimal value is 4 if and only if the $\oneinthree$ instance is satisfiable.
nodes.statement_short: Delete the constant $x_{\tau-4}$ so that the optimum of the resulting system is 4 exactly when the 1-in-3-SAT instance is satisfiable.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem ($\findoptstrength$ is \NP-hard)
nodes.statement_short: Turn each $\tau$-inequality of the TP(4,3) instance into a tile type with a matching cooperation set, so temperature 4 is achievable iff the SAT instance is satisfiable.

nodes.name: Proof of the $(n+c')h$ tile-type lower bound for the trees
nodes.statement: Being duplicated, each tree has its copy that assembles upward from the scaffold (actually, all trees but at most one do so since $\tas$ is assumed to be singly-seeded). Theorem~4.3 in \cite{AdChGoHuKeEsRo2002} implies that in order for $\tas$ to strictly self-assemble two variable trees of different types (e.g., north and west), at least $2h$ plus some constant number of tile types are necessary; $h$ exclusively for each, no matter how and at what temperature $\tas$ is designed, where the constant is much smaller than $h$. This is not to say that $\tas$ could not reuse any tile type for both of them. It can, for example, for their bit patterns. However, the number of such reusable tile types is bounded by a constant that is much smaller than $h$. This lower bound exists also for two trees of identical type but with distinct bit patterns. It is not allowed for $\tas$ to put tiles of identical type at the crotch positions because if they were the same, incorrect bit patterns could assemble. In contrast, $\tas$ is able to reuse tiles of same type for the cooperation tips of these trees, but anyway it saves only one tile type. This observation is immediately generalized for more variable and auxiliary trees as: in order for $\tas$ to assemble the $n$ distinct variable trees and $c'$ auxiliary trees, at least $(n+c')h + c''$ tile types are necessary for some constant $c'' \ll h$. In brief, \[ \dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge (n+c')h + c'' \] at {\it any temperature} $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Adleman et al.'s tree bound tree-by-tree: reuse across distinct trees is constant-bounded, so $(n+c')h + c''$ tile types are necessary at any temperature.

nodes.name: Proof that both copies share the cooperation-tip tile type
nodes.statement: This is related to the position of the seed of $\tas$ so that first we see that it merely costs the number of tile types for $\tas$ to put its head on a variable tree or an auxiliary tree. Suppose $\tas$ put its seed on one copy of some variable tree, and let us compare it with the other copy of the same tree. Recall that they are located next to each other. In order to start assembling the seed-free copy, $\tas$ first must assemble downward from the seed and the scaffold between the copies. Then consider the process for $\tas$ to assemble the seed-free copy upward up to the counterpart position of the seed. During this process, $\tas$ cannot reuse any tile type used for the part between the seed and scaffold; such a recycle would enable $\tas$ to skip the assembly of the seed-free copy and produce a shape with only one copy of the variable tree. Thus, even if the seed is on a copy of some variable tree, it could not be located ``far from'' the scaffold if it were not for extra $n$ tile types available for $\tas$. This means that $\tas$ needs to assemble almost all parts of these trees upward, and hence, it would impose the unaffordable number of extra tile types on $\tas$ to put tiles of distinct types at the cooperation tips of two copies of a tree.
nodes.statement_short: If the seed sat far from the scaffold, the seed-free copy could not reuse the seed-to-scaffold tile types, so distinct tip types would be unaffordable.

nodes.name: Proof of the first item of Property
nodes.statement: Now we will prove the first item of Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver}, that is, if the $\ge_\tau$-inequality \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau \end{equation} belongs to $\mathcal{S}$, then \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau, \end{equation} where $m \le 4$ and $k_1, \ldots, k_m \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Before that, however, let us quickly show that if \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} holds, then $\tas$ can assemble the logical component for \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality} by introducing only one new tile type in the following manner. $\tas$ first assembles the respective parts of the component that correspond to the variable trees for $v_{k_1}, \ldots, v_{k_m}$ as done for the copies of these trees (hence, costs nothing) and lets their cooperation tips to cooperate to attach a tile of the new type to fill the position surrounded by the $m$ cooperation tips, which is numbered 5 in the logical component in Figure~\ref{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}. This cooperation provides enough strength for stable tile attachment due to \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment}. Let us return to the proof. For the sake of contradiction, suppose \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} does not hold. Focus on the seed-free copy of the logical component for \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality} for the concise argumentation. Since this copy is free from seed, $\tas$ needs to assemble at least one pillar of the component upward from the scaffold. Under the supposition that \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} did not hold, $\tas$ is not allowed to assemble these upward-growing pillars as done for the corresponding variable trees without any extra tile types. More precisely, at the cooperation tip of at least one of these pillars, say the one for $v_{k_i}$, $\tas$ must put a tile of different type from $t_{k_i}$. However, this costs extra at least $h$ tile types because $\tau$ cannot reuse any tile types for the tree for $v_{k_i}$ in order to assemble this pillar, or any tile types for the any other tree $v_{k_j}$ because $\tas$ was proved not to be able to assemble $v_{k_i}$ and $v_{k_j}$ using strictly less than $2h$ tile types (this argument works in order to prove that this pillar cannot assemble using tile types for auxiliary trees).
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: if the glue sum fell short, some pillar of the seed-free logical component would need a fresh tip tile type, costing an unaffordable extra $h$ types.

nodes.name: Proof of the second item of Property
nodes.statement: Now we will prove that if \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_inequality} holds, then \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) < \tau. \end{equation} Before this proof, let us note that since the auxiliary tree does not appear in any other component, one can have $g$ assign an arbitrary strength to the glue at the cooperation tip of this tree without causing any malfunctioning of the other component, as long as \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment} holds. Setting this strength to be $\tau - \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j}$ enables $\tas$ to assemble this component with introducing only one new tile type that fills the position adjacent to the cooperation tips. For the sake of contradiction, suppose that the sum $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j)$ were at least $\tau$. Focus on the seed-free copy of this component, and especially first on the gadget with $m'+1$ pillars, with the position surrouned by the cooperation tips being filled (the leftmost gadget in Figure~\ref{fig:3vars_lessthan_tau}). Let us denote this gadget by $G_1$. Due to the seed-freeness, some of the pillars of $G_1$ assemble upward and have a tile $t$ fill the position by cooperative attachment. Assume that some pillar is absent from the cooperation. Let us denote the gadget that does not contain the ``lazy'' pillar by $G_2$. Then some of the tiles put at the cooperation tips of $G_2$ must be distinct from those at the corresponding positions of $G_1$ in type in order to prevent the tile $t$ from attaching to $G_2$. However, this distinctiveness would cost $\tas$ extra $h$ new tile types, as explained in the proof of the first item. Thus, all of the pillars of $G_1$ must join the cooperation, and hence, all the pillars of $G_1$ assemble upward. Then consider the gadget that is free from the auxiliary pillar, which we denote by $G_3$. The types of tiles at the corresponding cooperation tips of $G_1$ and $G_3$ must be the same in order for $\tas$ not to pay the unaffordable extra $h$ tile types. However, then there must exist $1 \le j \le m'$ such that the tile $t_j$ at the cooperation tip of the tree for $v_j$ and the tile at the corresponding position in $G_1$ must differ from each other in type because of the supposition $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) \ge \tau$. This again causes the unaffordable cost. Consequently, we can say that \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment} must hold.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction over the gadgets $G_1, G_2, G_3$ of the $<_\tau$-component: any tip-type mismatch forced by a glue sum $\ge \tau$ costs an unaffordable extra $h$ tile types.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorems on global behavior by instantiating the framework
nodes.statement: In order to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}, for $k \ge 2$, we choose the system of $\tau$-inequalities that cannot be solved for any $\tau < k$ but can for any $\tau \ge k$. This is the one designed in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries} based on the $2^{i+1}$-adders. It is transformed into a shape $S$ through Steps 2-4. This amounts to a proof of a slightly-stronger version of Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}. As for Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}, the TP instance built for Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} is rather chosen. In the rest of this section, therefore, we just have to verify Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver} in order to complete the proof of these theorems.
nodes.statement_short: Both theorems reduce to Property by choosing $\mathcal{S}$: the adder system for the temperature-preference theorem, the TP(4,3) instance for the \NP-hardness one.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma ($\dtilec{3}(S) < \dtilec{4}(S)$)
nodes.statement: As explained into details when being introduced, the framework needs only our appropriate choice of a system of $\tau$-inequalities at Step 1. Actually, it suffices to find as such a system the one that is solvable for $\tau = 3$ but not for $\tau = 4$. Such an equation, however, was already given as \eqref{eq:TP_example_1} in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries}. Needless to say, all $\ge_\tau$-inequalities and all $<_\tau$-inequalities in this system are of at most 4 and 3 terms, respectively, and this system is quadripartite.
nodes.statement_short: Feed the framework the system \eqref{eq:TP_example_1}, which is solvable at $\tau = 3$ but not at $\tau = 4$.

nodes.name: $\tau$-inequality system for a one-tile cooperation set
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &\ge& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_3 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_2 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_1 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \ell_2 + \ell_3 + \ell_4 &<& \tau \\ \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The five-inequality system whose minimum feasible $\tau$ is 4.

nodes.name: positivity pair \eqref{eq:positive}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_a \ge \tau \mbox{ and } x_a < \tau. \end{equation}

nodes.name: the $2^{i+1}$-adder inequality system
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{llll} A_1' + B_1' + x_0, & A_1'' + B_1'' + x_0 &\ge& \tau, \\ A_1 + B_1' + x_0, & A_1' + B_1'' + x_0 &<& \tau, \\ A_{j-1} + B_j' + A_j', & A_{j-1} + B_j'' + A_j'' &\ge& \tau, \\ A_{j-1}'' + B_j' + A_j, & A_j' + B_j'' + A_{j-1}'' &<& \tau, \\ A_i'' + x_b, & z_1 + x_c &<& \tau, \\ z_1 + x_b, & z_2 + x_c &\ge& \tau. \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Twelve three-term $\tau$-inequalities implementing the $2^{i+1}$-adder.

nodes.name: recurrence bound on $A_i''$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} A_i'' \ge A_i + 2^{i+1}-2 \end{equation}

nodes.name: 13-clause quadripartite conjunction
nodes.statement_short: The gadget replacing one 1-in-3 clause by thirteen clauses.

nodes.name: clause conversion \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conversion}
quartering of the variables of the 28-clause conjunction
clause encoding at $\tau = 4$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < 4, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < 4, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Four inequalities equivalent to $v_{j_1}+v_{j_2}+v_{j_3}=4$.

nodes.name: constant-forcing inequality \eqref{eq:tau-4}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 + x_{\tau{-}4} < \tau \end{equation}

nodes.name: clause encoding at general $\tau$
nodes.statement: \begin{eqnarray} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} + x_{\tau{-}4} &\ge& \tau, \\ v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + x_{\tau{-}4} &<& \tau, \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: inequality \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 < \tau, \end{equation}

nodes.name: clause inequalities for the TP instance
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < \tau, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < \tau. \end{equation}

nodes.name: the $\ge_\tau$-inequality \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le i \le m} v_{k_i} \ge \tau \end{equation}

nodes.name: the glue-strength counterpart \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le i \le m} g(\ell_{k_i}) \ge \tau, \end{equation}

nodes.name: the $<_\tau$-inequality \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_inequality}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j} < \tau \end{equation}

nodes.name: the glue-strength counterpart \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment}
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) < \tau. \end{equation}

nodes.name: tile-complexity lower bound for the tree part of $S$
nodes.statement: \[ \dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge (n+c')h + c'' \]

nodes.name: Set up the reduction from monotone \oneinthree
nodes.statement: Let us denote a given instance of monotone $\oneinthree$ by a pair of a set $U$ of Boolean variables and a set of clauses of three literals, which are positive due to the monotonicity. We will show a polynomial-time reduction from this to an instance of quadripartite $\oneinthree$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a monotone 1-in-3-SAT instance and announce a polynomial-time reduction to the quadripartite variant.

nodes.name: Replace each clause by the 13-clause gadget
nodes.statement_short: Convert clause $\{x,y,z\}$ into 13 clauses over fresh per-clause variables plus the negated literals.

nodes.name: Satisfiability is preserved in the case $x = 1, y = z = 0$
nodes.statement: We claim that this preserves the $\oneinthree$ satisfiability. If the $i$-th clause is $\oneinthree$ satisfied, then due to the symmetry among $x, y, z$ in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction}, it suffices to examine the case $x = 1, y = z = 0$. Then this conjunction is $\oneinthree$ satisfied by setting $a_1, d_x, e_{yz}, f_{xy}, f_{zx}$ to be 1 and the others to be 0.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry only $x=1, y=z=0$ needs checking, and an explicit assignment satisfies the gadget.

nodes.name: The case $x = y = z = 0$ fails
nodes.statement: If $x = y = z = 0$, then the first three clauses in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction} imply $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = 0$, but then the fourth clause cannot be satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: All-false forces $a_1=a_2=a_3=0$, which breaks the fourth clause.

nodes.name: The case $x = y = 1$ fails
nodes.statement: In the case $x = y = 1$, we consider two cases depending on the value of $c$. If $c = 0$, then $d_x = d_y = 1$ must hold in order to satisfy $\{\neg x, c, d_x\}$ and $\{\neg y, c, d_y\}$, but then the clause $\{d_x, d_y, e_{xy}\}$ contains too many true variables. Otherwise, $d_x = d_y = e_{xy} = 0$, but then the clause cannot be satisfied. Therefore, the clause $\{x, y, z\}$ is $\oneinthree$ satisfiable if and only if so are all clauses in \eqref{eq:quad_1in3SAT_conjunction}.
nodes.statement_short: Both values of $c$ break a clause, completing the equivalence.

nodes.name: Iterate the four-clause conversion to reach quadripartiteness
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the last clause with the auxiliary conversion and reapply it to remove mixed literals.

nodes.name: Exhibit the quartering of the 28-clause conjunction
nodes.statement:
In this way, we finally obtain a conjunction of 28 clauses that admits quartering its variables as follows:  egin{eqnarray*} U_{i,1} &=& \{
eg x, 
eg y, 
eg z, e_{xy}, e_{yz}, e_{zx}\}, \ U_{i,2} &=& \{a_1, b_3, c\}, \ U_{i,3} &=& \{a_2, b_1, d_x, d_z, f_{xy}, f_{yz}, f_{zx}\}, \ U_{i,4} &=& \{a_3, b_2, d_y\}, \end{eqnarray*} where the variables introduced via the conversion of last clause are omitted. Observe that the (negated) literals of all variables in the given SAT instance is in the same set $U_{i, 1}$, and that $(U_{i, 2} \cup U_{i, 3} \cup U_{i, 4}) \cap (U_{j, 2} \cup U_{j, 3} \cup U_{j, 4}) = \emptyset$ for any $1 \le i < j \le n$. These two properties immediately bring us the quartering of variables occurring in the resulting conjunction as $U_k =  igcup_{1 \le i \le n} U_{i, k}$ for each $k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The per-clause quartering unions into a global four-way partition, so the instance is quadripartite.

nodes.name: Reduce quadripartite \oneinthree, starting at $\tau = 4$
nodes.statement: A proof for $\tau=4$ comes first. An instance of quadripartite\footnote{The quadripartite property is not needed here, but will be so in Section~\ref{sec:complexity}.} $\oneinthree$, whose \NP-completeness was proved in Lemma~\ref{lem:quad_1in3SAT}, will be reduced into an instance of $\tau$-TP(4,~3). Let us represent this instance as a pair of a set of Boolean variables $U = \{u_1, \ldots, u_n\}$ and that of clauses $C = \{c_1, \ldots, c_m\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Start from a quadripartite 1-in-3-SAT instance and name its variables and clauses.

nodes.name: Encode each clause as four $\tau$-inequalities
nodes.statement: Let us convert this SAT instance into a system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities with positive integer variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ (needless to say, \eqref{eq:positive} is used here for their positiveness), which correspond to the SAT variables in $U$, such that the SAT instance is satisfiable if and only if the system is solvable. In $\mathcal{S}$, the $j$-th clause of $C$, $c_j = \{u_{j_1}, u_{j_2}, u_{j_3}\}$ with $1 \le j_1, j_2, j_3 \le n$, is represented as \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < 4, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < 4, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < 4, \end{equation} which is equivalent to the equation $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$ due to the assumption that $v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3} \ge 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce a positive variable per SAT variable and encode clause $c_j$ by \eqref{eq:clause_4}.

nodes.name: Read off the truth assignment and conclude for $\tau = 4$
nodes.statement: Its solution must be that exactly one of the three variables is 2 and the others are 1. Therefore, if $\mathcal{S}$ is solvable, then by interpreting those in $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ with value 2 be positive and the other (that is, with value 1) negative, we can retrieve a way to satisfy the $\oneinthree$ instance; and vice versa. Thus, 4-TP(4, 3) is \NP-complete (in fact, we proved that even 4-TP(3, 2) is so, see \eqref{eq:clause_4}).
nodes.statement_short: Value 2 means true and 1 means false, giving \NP-completeness of 4-TP(4,3).

nodes.name: Embed adders to force the constants $x_1, x_2, x_{\tau-4}$
nodes.statement: Now the result is generalized for an arbitrary $\tau \ge 4$. In $\mathcal{S}$, we first embed systems of $\tau$-inequalities of at most three terms, presented in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries}, that provide auxiliary variables $x_1, x_2, x_{\tau{-}4}$ with lower bounds 1, 2, and $\tau{-}4$, respectively. Combining them with an inequality \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 + x_{\tau{-}4} < \tau \end{equation} yields $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 2$, and $x_{\tau{-}4} = \tau{-}4$. This means that by \eqref{eq:tau-4} being embedded, in any solution of $\mathcal{S}$, these variables must admit these respective values.
nodes.statement_short: Adder sub-systems plus \eqref{eq:tau-4} pin the auxiliary variables to $1$, $2$ and $\tau-4$.

nodes.name: Add the constant $x_{\tau-4}$ to the clause inequalities
nodes.statement: Especially, the ``constant'' $x_{\tau{-}4}$ is added to the inequalities in \eqref{eq:clause_4}, and we obtain \begin{eqnarray} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} + x_{\tau{-}4} &\ge& \tau, \\ v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + x_{\tau{-}4} &<& \tau, \end{eqnarray} and the analogs of \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} for $v_{j_1} + v_{j_3}$ and $v_{j_2} + v_{j_3}$. Since $x_{\tau-4} = \tau-4$, these four $\tau$-inequalities are equivalent to $v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} = 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting by $\tau-4$ keeps the clause constraint equivalent to the sum being 4.

nodes.name: Check the term counts and quadripartiteness
nodes.statement: We conclude this proof by noting that any $\tau$-inequality used is either a $\ge_\tau$-inequality of at most 4 terms or a $<_\tau$-inequality of at most 3 terms, and the resulting system of $\tau$-inequalities is quadripartite. This quadripartite property will become critical in proving Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}.
nodes.statement_short: Every inequality lies in TP(4,3) and the whole system is quadripartite.

nodes.name: Delete the constant term to obtain the TP instance
nodes.statement: Deleting the constant term $x_{\tau-4}$ from the inequalities \eqref{eq:tau-4}, \eqref{eq:clause_atleast_tau}, and \eqref{eq:clause_lessthan_tau} yields the following inequalities: \begin{equation} x_1 + x_2 < \tau, \end{equation} \begin{equation} v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} \ge \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_2} < \tau, v_{j_1} + v_{j_3} < \tau, \mbox{ and } v_{j_2} + v_{j_3} < \tau. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Dropping $x_{\tau-4}$ turns the fixed-$\tau$ system into a genuine TP instance.

nodes.name: The minimum possible $\tau$ is 4
nodes.statement: Consider optimizing $\tau$ subject to these. Due to \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2}, the minimal possible value of $\tau$ is 4.
nodes.statement_short: \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2} bounds the optimum from below by 4.

nodes.name: The optimum equals 4 exactly on satisfiable instances
nodes.statement: Then its optimal value is 4 if and only if the $\oneinthree$ instance is satisfiable.
nodes.statement_short: Optimality at 4 is equivalent to satisfiability, so TP(4,3) is \NP-hard.

nodes.name: Transform the $\tau$-inequalities into cooperation sets
nodes.statement: Making use of the fact that all of its $\tau$-inequalities contain at most 4 terms, we transform them into cooperation sets of a strength-free TAS.
nodes.statement_short: At most 4 terms per inequality lets each inequality become one tile side pattern.

nodes.name: Encode the clause inequalities as a tile type $t_{c_j}$
nodes.statement_short: Clause $c_j$ becomes $t_{c_j} = (v_{j_1}, v_{j_2}, v_{j_3}, x_\tau)$ with the matching cooperation set.

nodes.name: Encode the positivity inequalities as tile types $t_i$
nodes.statement: Likewise, the inequalities that aim at forcing $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ be positive are converted. The inequalities in \eqref{eq:positive} are encoded as a tile type $t_i = (x_1, x_a, x_\tau, x_\tau)$ with $\mathcal{D}(t_i) = \mathcal{P}(\{\north, \west, \south, \east\}) \setminus \{\{\north\}, \{\west\}\}$. Though being not mentioned in \eqref{eq:positive}, we can assume $x_1 < \tau$ as noted in Remark~\ref{rmk:strictly_lessthan_tau}.
nodes.statement_short: \eqref{eq:positive} becomes $t_i = (x_1, x_a, x_\tau, x_\tau)$, using $x_1 < \tau$ from the Remark.

nodes.name: Encode \eqref{eq:TP_x1x2} as the tile type $t'$
nodes.statement_short: The remaining constant-forcing inequality becomes one more tile type.

nodes.name: Temperature 4 is achievable iff the SAT instance is satisfiable
nodes.statement: Then, there exists a TAS at temperature 4 that is locally equivalent to this strength-free TAS if and only if the given instance of $\oneinthree$ is satisfiable.
nodes.statement_short: The reduction is complete, so minimizing the temperature is \NP-hard.

nodes.name: Every tree has an upward-growing copy
nodes.statement: Being duplicated, each tree has its copy that assembles upward from the scaffold (actually, all trees but at most one do so since $\tas$ is assumed to be singly-seeded).
nodes.statement_short: Duplication plus single-seededness guarantees a seed-free copy of each tree.

nodes.name: Apply Adleman et al.'s tree lower bound
nodes.statement: Theorem~4.3 in \cite{AdChGoHuKeEsRo2002} implies that in order for $\tas$ to strictly self-assemble two variable trees of different types (e.g., north and west), at least $2h$ plus some constant number of tile types are necessary; $h$ exclusively for each, no matter how and at what temperature $\tas$ is designed, where the constant is much smaller than $h$.
nodes.statement_short: Two trees of different types cost at least $2h$ tile types, $h$ each.

nodes.name: Bound the reusable tile types by a constant
nodes.statement: This is not to say that $\tas$ could not reuse any tile type for both of them. It can, for example, for their bit patterns. However, the number of such reusable tile types is bounded by a constant that is much smaller than $h$. This lower bound exists also for two trees of identical type but with distinct bit patterns. It is not allowed for $\tas$ to put tiles of identical type at the crotch positions because if they were the same, incorrect bit patterns could assemble. In contrast, $\tas$ is able to reuse tiles of same type for the cooperation tips of these trees, but anyway it saves only one tile type.
nodes.statement_short: Reuse is limited to bit patterns and tips; crotch tiles must differ, so savings are $O(1)$.

nodes.name: Generalize to all $n + c'$ trees
nodes.statement: This observation is immediately generalized for more variable and auxiliary trees as: in order for $\tas$ to assemble the $n$ distinct variable trees and $c'$ auxiliary trees, at least $(n+c')h + c''$ tile types are necessary for some constant $c'' \ll h$. In brief, \[ \dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge (n+c')h + c'' \] at {\it any temperature} $\tau$.
nodes.statement_short: Summing over trees gives $\dtilec{\tau}(S) \ge (n+c')h + c''$ at any temperature.

nodes.name: Compare the seeded and seed-free copies of a tree
nodes.statement: This is related to the position of the seed of $\tas$ so that first we see that it merely costs the number of tile types for $\tas$ to put its head on a variable tree or an auxiliary tree. Suppose $\tas$ put its seed on one copy of some variable tree, and let us compare it with the other copy of the same tree. Recall that they are located next to each other.
nodes.statement_short: Put the seed on one copy and compare it with its neighbouring twin.

nodes.name: No tile type can be reused between seed and scaffold
nodes.statement: In order to start assembling the seed-free copy, $\tas$ first must assemble downward from the seed and the scaffold between the copies. Then consider the process for $\tas$ to assemble the seed-free copy upward up to the counterpart position of the seed. During this process, $\tas$ cannot reuse any tile type used for the part between the seed and scaffold; such a recycle would enable $\tas$ to skip the assembly of the seed-free copy and produce a shape with only one copy of the variable tree.
nodes.statement_short: Reusing those tile types would let $\tas$ skip the second copy and assemble a wrong shape.

nodes.name: Conclude that both tips carry the same tile type
nodes.statement: Thus, even if the seed is on a copy of some variable tree, it could not be located ``far from'' the scaffold if it were not for extra $n$ tile types available for $\tas$. This means that $\tas$ needs to assemble almost all parts of these trees upward, and hence, it would impose the unaffordable number of extra tile types on $\tas$ to put tiles of distinct types at the cooperation tips of two copies of a tree.
nodes.statement_short: The seed must stay near the scaffold, so distinct tip types would be unaffordable.

nodes.name: Sufficiency: one new tile type fills the shared position
nodes.statement: Before that, however, let us quickly show that if \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} holds, then $\tas$ can assemble the logical component for \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality} by introducing only one new tile type in the following manner. $\tas$ first assembles the respective parts of the component that correspond to the variable trees for $v_{k_1}, \ldots, v_{k_m}$ as done for the copies of these trees (hence, costs nothing) and lets their cooperation tips to cooperate to attach a tile of the new type to fill the position surrounded by the $m$ cooperation tips, which is numbered 5 in the logical component in Figure~\ref{fig:4vars_atleast_tau}. This cooperation provides enough strength for stable tile attachment due to \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment}.
nodes.statement_short: If the glue strengths already sum to $\tau$, one fresh tile type completes the component for free.

nodes.name: Assume the glue sum falls short
nodes.statement: Let us return to the proof. For the sake of contradiction, suppose \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} does not hold. Focus on the seed-free copy of the logical component for \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_inequality} for the concise argumentation.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose the strengths do not reach $\tau$ and work in the seed-free copy.

nodes.name: Some pillar needs a different tip tile type
nodes.statement: Since this copy is free from seed, $\tas$ needs to assemble at least one pillar of the component upward from the scaffold. Under the supposition that \eqref{eq:at_least_tau_attachment} did not hold, $\tas$ is not allowed to assemble these upward-growing pillars as done for the corresponding variable trees without any extra tile types. More precisely, at the cooperation tip of at least one of these pillars, say the one for $v_{k_i}$, $\tas$ must put a tile of different type from $t_{k_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: The upward-growing pillars cannot copy the variable trees, so a tip type must change.

nodes.name: The change costs an unaffordable extra $h$ tile types
nodes.statement: However, this costs extra at least $h$ tile types because $\tau$ cannot reuse any tile types for the tree for $v_{k_i}$ in order to assemble this pillar, or any tile types for the any other tree $v_{k_j}$ because $\tas$ was proved not to be able to assemble $v_{k_i}$ and $v_{k_j}$ using strictly less than $2h$ tile types (this argument works in order to prove that this pillar cannot assemble using tile types for auxiliary trees).
nodes.statement_short: No tree's tile types can be recycled, so the cost exceeds the budget — contradiction.

nodes.name: Sufficiency: tune the auxiliary tip strength
nodes.statement: Before this proof, let us note that since the auxiliary tree does not appear in any other component, one can have $g$ assign an arbitrary strength to the glue at the cooperation tip of this tree without causing any malfunctioning of the other component, as long as \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment} holds. Setting this strength to be $\tau - \sum_{1 \le j \le m'} v_{k_j}$ enables $\tas$ to assemble this component with introducing only one new tile type that fills the position adjacent to the cooperation tips.
nodes.statement_short: Set the auxiliary glue to $\tau - \sum v_{k_j}$ so one new tile type completes the component.

nodes.name: Assume the glue sum reaches $\tau$ and isolate $G_1$
nodes.statement: For the sake of contradiction, suppose that the sum $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j)$ were at least $\tau$. Focus on the seed-free copy of this component, and especially first on the gadget with $m'+1$ pillars, with the position surrouned by the cooperation tips being filled (the leftmost gadget in Figure~\ref{fig:3vars_lessthan_tau}). Let us denote this gadget by $G_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose the strengths reach $\tau$ and focus on the full $(m'+1)$-pillar gadget.

nodes.name: All pillars of $G_1$ must join the cooperation
nodes.statement: Due to the seed-freeness, some of the pillars of $G_1$ assemble upward and have a tile $t$ fill the position by cooperative attachment. Assume that some pillar is absent from the cooperation. Let us denote the gadget that does not contain the ``lazy'' pillar by $G_2$. Then some of the tiles put at the cooperation tips of $G_2$ must be distinct from those at the corresponding positions of $G_1$ in type in order to prevent the tile $t$ from attaching to $G_2$. However, this distinctiveness would cost $\tas$ extra $h$ new tile types, as explained in the proof of the first item. Thus, all of the pillars of $G_1$ must join the cooperation, and hence, all the pillars of $G_1$ assemble upward.
nodes.statement_short: A lazy pillar would force distinct tip types in $G_2$, costing an extra $h$ tile types.

nodes.name: Comparing with $G_3$ forces a mismatch
nodes.statement: Then consider the gadget that is free from the auxiliary pillar, which we denote by $G_3$. The types of tiles at the corresponding cooperation tips of $G_1$ and $G_3$ must be the same in order for $\tas$ not to pay the unaffordable extra $h$ tile types. However, then there must exist $1 \le j \le m'$ such that the tile $t_j$ at the cooperation tip of the tree for $v_j$ and the tile at the corresponding position in $G_1$ must differ from each other in type because of the supposition $\sum_{1 \le j \le m'} g(\ell_j) \ge \tau$. This again causes the unaffordable cost.
nodes.statement_short: Matching $G_3$'s tips makes some variable tree's tip differ from $G_1$'s — again unaffordable.

nodes.name: Conclude the $<_\tau$ glue inequality
nodes.statement: Consequently, we can say that \eqref{eq:less_than_tau_attachment} must hold.
nodes.statement_short: Hence the glue strengths must stay strictly below $\tau$.

nodes.name: Choose the adder system for the temperature-preference theorem
nodes.statement: In order to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}, for $k \ge 2$, we choose the system of $\tau$-inequalities that cannot be solved for any $\tau < k$ but can for any $\tau \ge k$. This is the one designed in Section~\ref{subsec:TP_preliminaries} based on the $2^{i+1}$-adders. It is transformed into a shape $S$ through Steps 2-4. This amounts to a proof of a slightly-stronger version of Theorem~\ref{thm:tau_better_than_less}.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate Step 1 with the adder system, solvable exactly for $\tau \ge k$.

nodes.name: Choose the TP(4,3) instance for the \NP-hardness theorem
nodes.statement: As for Theorem~\ref{thm:TC_above_4_NPhard}, the TP instance built for Theorem~\ref{thm:4TP_NP-complete} is rather chosen.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate Step 1 with the SAT-encoding TP(4,3) instance instead.

nodes.name: Reduce both theorems to verifying Property
nodes.statement: In the rest of this section, therefore, we just have to verify Property~\ref{property:TAS_as_inequality_system_solver} in order to complete the proof of these theorems.
nodes.statement_short: Only the Property remains to be verified.

nodes.name: Step 1: choose a quadripartite $\tau$-inequality system
nodes.statement: choose a quadripartite system $\mathcal{S}$ of $\tau$-inequalities properly for the purpose among those built in Section~\ref{sec:behavior}; hence, all $\ge_\tau$-inequalities of $\mathcal{S}$ are of at most 4 terms and all of its $<_\tau$-inequalities are of at most 3 terms;
nodes.statement_short: Select $\mathcal{S}$ from Section 3 so that $\ge_\tau$-inequalities have $\le 4$ terms and $<_\tau$-inequalities $\le 3$.

nodes.name: Step 2: convert variables into variable trees
nodes.statement: convert its variables $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$ into trees of height $h$ and distinct shape, which we call {\it variable trees}, where $h$ is a parameter adjustable for our convenience;
nodes.statement_short: Turn each variable into a distinctly shaped height-$h$ tree.

nodes.name: Step 3: bundle trees into logical components
nodes.statement: for each $\tau$-inequality, bundle the (at most 4) trees thus converted from its variables into a shape called the {\it logical component};
nodes.statement_short: Bundle each inequality's trees so their cooperation tips surround one position.

nodes.name: Step 4: mount two copies of everything on a scaffold
nodes.statement: (two copies of) the $n$ variable trees and logical components each are mounted next to each other onto a scaffold, and amounts to a shape, which we denote by $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Mount two copies of every tree and component on a scaffold to obtain the shape $S$.
